subject: biochemistry
title: Epigenetic mechanisms, chromatin remodeling, and transcriptional regulation

steps.tx: Gene expression in multicellular organisms is fundamentally governed by **chromatin** structure. Genomic DNA wraps around octamers of core histones (H2A, H2B, H3, H4) to form nucleosomes. Dense, transcriptionally silent heterochromatin resists transcription factor access, whereas relaxed, open euchromatin facilitates gene activation. Histone acetyltransferases add acetyl groups to basic lysine tails, neutralizing positive charges and loosening histone-DNA electrostatic interactions.
steps.say: Chromatin structure regulates genomic accessibility. DNA wraps around histone octamers forming nucleosomes. Condensed heterochromatin is transcriptionally inert, whereas open euchromatin permits transcription factor binding. Histone acetyltransferases neutralize lysine charges to relax chromatin.

steps.tx: Histone acetyltransferases relax chromatin into euchromatin, permitting active gene transcription. Conversely, DNA methylation and histone deacetylation compact DNA into transcriptionally silent heterochromatin. steps.tx: DNA **methylation** constitutes a stable, heritable epigenetic mark. DNA methyltransferases transfer methyl groups from S-adenosylmethionine onto cytosine bases within CpG dinucleotide islands located in gene promoters. Methylated CpG motifs recruit methyl-CpG-binding domain proteins (MeCP2) that recruit histone deacetylases, cementing transcriptional silencing. Rett syndrome is caused by loss-of-function mutations in MeCP2, causing progressive neurodevelopmental regression in young girls.
steps.say: DNA methyltransferases transfer methyl groups to promoter CpG islands, recruiting MeCP2 and histone deacetylases to maintain gene silencing. Mutations in MeCP2 cause Rett syndrome, characterized by neurodevelopmental regression and hand-wringing stereotypic movements.

steps.tx: Genomic **imprinting** represents parent-of-origin specific gene expression mediated by differential DNA methylation. In Prader-Willi syndrome, deletion or maternal uniparental disomy of the paternal 15q11-q13 region deprives the patient of paternally expressed genes, resulting in neonatal hypotonia and compulsive hyperphagia. Conversely, deletion or paternal uniparental disomy of the maternal 15q11-q13 locus (inactivating the maternal UBE3A ubiquitin ligase) produces Angelman syndrome, manifesting with paroxysmal laughter and ataxia.
steps.say: Genomic imprinting selectively silences maternal or paternal alleles via methylation. Loss of paternal 15q11-q13 produces Prader-Willi syndrome with hyperphagia, while loss of maternal 15q11-q13 UBE3A yields Angelman syndrome with ataxia and inappropriate laughter.

steps.tx: Epigenetic therapies provide potent **antineoplastic** tools. DNA hypomethylating agents like 5-azacitidine and decitabine incorporate into DNA, trapping DNA methyltransferases and re-activating silenced tumor suppressor genes in myelodysplastic syndromes. Histone deacetylase inhibitors like vorinostat and romidepsin promote hyperacetylation of histone lysines, forcing chromatin relaxation and inducing cell cycle arrest in cutaneous T-cell lymphomas.
steps.say: Hypomethylating agents azacitidine and decitabine trap DNA methyltransferases to reactivate silenced tumor suppressors in myelodysplastic syndromes. Histone deacetylase inhibitors like vorinostat enforce hyperacetylation, treating cutaneous T-cell lymphoma.
